headline: Highest risk is medium: ms-swift can write/execute locally while pathway is read-only, so prompt-injection and data-leak paths are limited but not absent.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: ms-swift can read/write files and process stdin/stdout, so if pathway outputs are manually or file-bridged into it, prompt injection is possible. pathway has no file or clipboard surfaces, so there is no default automated bridge. The pathway is low because the interaction needs unusual bridging, not a built-in channel.
conditions: IF pathway outputs are copied into ms-swift prompts or files, injected instructions can be interpreted.
IF an operator creates a shared file bridge between the agents, prompt content can be hijacked.
mitigations: Keep the agents on separate workspaces.
Do not paste pathway outputs directly into ms-swift prompts.
Strip instructions from any shared text before reuse.
Use a fixed prompt template for ms-swift.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging on any shared artifacts.

B_data_leakage.rationale: ms-swift touches files, logs, checkpoints, and secrets such as hub_token/sdk-token, while pathway exposes no filesystem, clipboard, or API egress surfaces. That makes leakage plausible only through operator-mediated sharing or local workspace overlap, not by default agent-to-agent transfer. The blast radius is limited to the shared artifacts involved.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same directory, ms-swift artifacts may be exposed to pathway-adjacent workflows.
IF secrets are stored in files that are later shared, they can leak through manual handling.
mitigations: Store secrets outside shared folders.
Use separate directories for each agent.
Rotate any token written to disk.
Review logs before sharing them.
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent filesystem isolation.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: ms-swift can write the filesystem and spawn subprocesses, but it cannot modify git state; pathway cannot write files or spawn processes. Overlapping mutable-resource conflict is therefore limited, and the pair lacks the high-risk same-dir git or unrestricted dual-write pattern described by the rubric.
conditions: IF both agents are manually pointed at the same writable directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF an external orchestrator grants pathway write access, conflicts become more likely.
mitigations: Assign distinct output directories.
Avoid concurrent writes to shared files.
Run one agent at a time for mutable artifacts.
Snapshot files before edits.
requires-engineering: add locking around shared resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: ms-swift can generate outputs from files and stdin/stdout, and pathway is a document-processing system that may consume upstream outputs. If pathway treats ms-swift text as authoritative, errors can cascade into downstream work products. The interaction is inferred rather than directly documented, so uncertainty pushes this to medium.
conditions: IF pathway ingests ms-swift-generated text without verification, upstream mistakes propagate.
IF ms-swift is used to draft facts that pathway later renders or routes, errors can cascade.
mitigations: Add a human review step before downstream use.
Require schema validation on ms-swift outputs.
Mark generated text as untrusted.
Compare outputs against source files.
requires-engineering: implement verification gates in the pipeline.

E_compliance.rationale: ms-swift explicitly handles hub_token and sdk-token and may write logs, checkpoints, and configuration files, while pathway exposes no stated retention or residency controls. The pair therefore has a compliance gap only if sensitive data is routed into shared artifacts; pathway is not cited for a specific violation because its compliance posture is not documented here.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in ms-swift logs or checkpoints and then shared onward, retention risk arises.
IF pathway is deployed in a jurisdiction with stricter residency rules than ms-swift's storage location, mismatch occurs.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of logs.
Purge checkpoints after use.
Separate storage by jurisdiction.
Document retention for shared artifacts.
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for data residency and retention.
